title: Pressure-cooker cheesecake
subtitle: A creamy, crack-free cheesecake baked in steam
excerpt: A classic cream cheese cheesecake cooked under pressure in a water bath, no cracks, no over-baking, and a silkier texture than oven-baked versions. Requires a 18 cm springform tin that fits your pressure cooker.
sourceNotes: Pressure-cooker cheesecake became popular through electric pressure cooker communities in the 2010s. The steam environment of a pressure cooker is functionally similar to a water bath in an oven, a gentle, humid heat that cooks the cheesecake without cracking the surface.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze whole or in slices, wrapped tightly, for up to 2 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The cheesecake must be made at least 4 hours ahead (ideally overnight) to set fully in the fridge before slicing.

content.text: Pressure-cooker cheesecake is the solution to cracked oven bakes. Steam inside the pot cooks the cheesecake gently and evenly. The effect is the same as a water bath, without the setup. The result is a smooth top, no cracks, and a dense, creamy interior.

The tin must fit inside your pressure cooker with the lid on, measure carefully before you begin. An 18 cm springform tin fits most 6-litre and larger pressure cookers. The tin sits on a trivet above the water level inside the pot.

All filling ingredients must be at room temperature before starting. Cold cream cheese will not mix smoothly and produces a lumpy, uneven texture. Remove everything from the fridge at least 2 hours before you begin.

Line the base of an 18 cm springform tin with baking paper. Mix the crushed digestive biscuits with the melted butter until combined. Press firmly into the base of the tin in an even layer. Refrigerate for 15 minutes while you make the filling.

Beat the cream cheese and caster sugar together with an electric hand whisk until smooth. Add the eggs one at a time, beating briefly after each addition. Add the yoghurt, vanilla extract, and lemon juice. Mix until smooth. Do not overbeat, this incorporates air that causes cracking.

Pour the filling over the chilled base. Cover the tin tightly with foil, shiny side down, to prevent condensation dripping onto the surface. Add 300 ml of water to the pressure cooker and place the trivet inside. Lower the tin onto the trivet. Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 30 minutes. Allow a full natural pressure release of at least 20 minutes before opening.

Lift the tin out carefully. Remove the foil, the cheesecake will look slightly wobbly in the centre, which is correct. Allow to cool at room temperature for 1 hour, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight. The cheesecake sets as it chills. Remove from the tin and serve.

rows.symptom: The cheesecake centre is still liquid after the full cook time
rows.cause: The tin size was different, or the pressure cooker did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 5 minutes. The cheesecake will continue to set as it chills, a slightly wobbly centre when warm is normal.

rows.cause: The foil was not sealed tightly and condensation dripped onto the cheesecake.
rows.fix: This does not affect texture or flavour. Dab gently with kitchen paper. For next time, crimp the foil tightly under the rim of the tin.

rows.cause: The cream cheese was cold when used.
rows.fix: Always use cream cheese at room temperature. Press through a fine sieve if lumps remain in the uncooked filling.

content.text: New York-style cheesecake became popular in Britain through American influence in the second half of the 20th century. The pressure cooker version is easier than the oven method. No water bath to set up, no risk of a wet base, and no cracking from uneven heat. It suits a dinner party or a weekend bake where the overnight chill is part of the plan.
